text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT

- Finland can play for time in lifting its tight regulations on alcohol imports. Finnish alcohol regulations must conform to the EU's by the end of the year, but talks with the European Commission are stalled.
-Finnish coaches say too serious an approach to competition explains Finnish atheletes' poor performance at the Atlanta Olympics. They say atlethes should compete with a smile. @
- Foreigners, especially Russians, driving in Finland are more accident-prone than Finns, study shows.
- European Parliament elections do not deal with issues which affect ordinary people's lives, says Europarliament speaker Klaus Hansch.
KAUPPALEHTI
- Bank of Finland researcher Sinimaaria Ranki says EMU gets blamed for many problems, including unemployment, for which it is not responsible. @
- Forestry group Enso has put together borrowing programmes of 1.5 billion dollars, surpassing earlier borrowing of 600 million dollars by its predecessor company Enso-Gutzeit.

- Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said surplus cash in state coffers can only be used to reduce state debt, rejecting economics professor Jouko Paunio's suggestion that the money should be used for job-creating investment projects
- Phone company consortium Finnet-yhtiot plans to launch ticket booking agency to compete with Telecom Finland's Lippupalvelu. @
DEMARI
- Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said Finland had nothing to apologise for in its cold war past.
- Government divided over permit to export munitions parts to Israel.
AAMULEHTI

- Member of the European Parliament and U.N. human rights raporteur Elisabeth Rehn urged Finland to formulate a clearer policy on the use of land mines and to find out what the alternatives would cost.
- Birds' autumn migration now in full swing. @
- Ministerial group is not worried about concentration of power in the media. Ruutunelonen, controlled by Helsinki Media, is said to be strong candidate to get commercial TV licence.
- The use of 14 currencies in the EU costs member states 120 billion markka per year, said European Parliament speaker Klaus Hansch in Helsinki.
